_about: Study sheet: quick cards (shown in this order) and extra glossary terms live here; the other glossary terms come from data/mech-text.json (one copy only). Examples must work in Predict (tests/reactions.test.mjs checks each one gives its card's pathway as major). Rows are [label, text]. For which pathway wins, cards point to the grid built from rules.json instead of repeating the rules.
intro: Quick cards for the four mechanisms and Ch 7 alkenes, then the glossary. Search finds both. “Which pathway wins?” on the Reactions tab has the full decision table.

cards.title: SN2
rows: Rate = k[substrate][Nu]: bimolecular (both in the slow step).
One step, concerted: Nu bonds as the leaving group leaves. One transition state, no intermediate.
Methyl > 1° > 2°. 3° doesn't react (backside blocked). Neopentyl is very slow. Vinyl/aryl: no.
Strong nucleophile: I⁻, Br⁻, CN⁻, N₃⁻, RS⁻, HO⁻, RO⁻.
Polar aprotic (DMSO, DMF, acetone, CH₃CN) is best: it doesn't cage the Nu.
Inversion at the carbon (Walden, backside attack). Stereospecific: (R) gives the inverted product.
A strong base at 2° gives mostly E2. A bulky base (t-BuO⁻) gives E2 even at 1°.

cards.title: SN1
rows: Rate = k[substrate]: unimolecular (only the substrate in the slow step).
1) LG leaves → carbocation (slow). 2) Nu attacks C⁺. 3) Proton transfer if the Nu was neutral (H₂O, ROH).
3° > 2°; allylic and benzylic are good (resonance). 1° and methyl: no (cation too unstable).
Weak nucleophile, often the solvent (H₂O, ROH): solvolysis.
Polar protic (water, alcohols): stabilises the cation and the leaving anion.
The flat C⁺ is attacked from both faces: racemic (or a mixture) at that carbon.
Yes: a 1,2-H or alkyl shift (or ring expansion) if it gives a more stable cation.
With HBr/HCl, OH is protonated to OH₂⁺ and water leaves (2° and 3°).
E1 always competes (same cation). Heat pushes it toward E1.

cards.title: E2
rows: One step, concerted: the base takes a β-H, the C=C forms and the LG leaves together.
3° > 2° > 1° with a strong base. 1° needs a bulky base to beat SN2.
Strong base: HO⁻, RO⁻ (EtO⁻, MeO⁻), t-BuO⁻, DBU.
The β-H must be anti-periplanar (180°) to the LG. In a cyclohexane: both axial (trans-diaxial). Check it in the Newman and Chair tabs.
Small base → Zaitsev (more substituted). Bulky base (t-BuO⁻) → Hofmann (less substituted).
Stereospecific: if the β-carbon has one H, the configuration decides E or Z. Otherwise E (trans) is usually major.

cards.title: E1
rows: 1) LG leaves → carbocation (slow). 2) A weak base (H₂O, ROH, HSO₄⁻) takes a β-H → C=C.
3° > 2° (allylic/benzylic good). 1°: no. Alcohols: OH is protonated first by H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄ (dehydration).
Weak base, or acid with heat (H₂SO₄, H₃PO₄, TsOH).
No anti-periplanar rule: the flat C⁺ can lose any β-H.
Zaitsev: the more substituted (more stable) alkene; trans over cis.
Yes: shifts to a more stable cation before the H⁺ is lost.
Heat favours E1 over SN1 (more molecules made: entropy).

cards.title: Alkene stability
cards.sub: Ch 7: which alkene is more stable?
rows: C=C–C=C (conjugated) is more stable than isolated C=C's.
More carbons on the C=C is more stable: tetra > tri > di > mono. Each alkyl group donates a little electron density (hyperconjugation).
A C=C in or on a 3- or 4-membered ring is strained (less stable).
A C=C inside a ring beats one sticking out of it (exocyclic), at equal substitution.
Trans (E, big groups apart) beats cis (crowded).
Heat of hydrogenation: the less heat released when adding H₂, the more stable the alkene (compare isomers only).
Reactions tab, two or more alkenes in the editor → Rank alkenes by stability.

cards.title: E2 geometry
rows: Look down Cα–Cβ. Turn the back carbon until an H is anti (180°) to the LG. Groups anti in that shape end up trans; gauche ones end up cis.
If Cβ has two H's, both E and Z can form; the lower-energy shape (big groups apart) gives the major one, usually E.
Only one shape can react, so only one alkene forms: draw the Newman projection to see which.
LG must be axial, with an axial H on the next ring carbon (trans-diaxial). A ring flip may be needed; if the flipped chair is very strained, E2 is slow.
If the only anti H is on the less substituted side, that alkene forms (e.g. menthyl chloride).
Molecule tab → Newman (open chains) or Chair (rings). Predict's green note says which shape reacts.

cards.title: Leaving groups
cards.sub: What leaves, and how to make OH leave
rows: Weak bases: I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ ≫ F⁻ (poor). TsO⁻, MsO⁻ (sulfonates) are excellent. H₂O is good.
HO⁻ is a strong base, so an alcohol must be activated first.
Protonates OH to OH₂⁺; water leaves. Gives a carbocation at 2°/3° (rearrangements possible).
Turn OH into Br or Cl by SN2 at 1°/2°: no carbocation, no rearrangement; inversion at the carbon.
Turns OH into OTs. The C–O bond isn't broken: retention. Then do SN2 or E2 on the OTs.

reagentCard.sub: Spot the type, then you know what it does

glossary.Newman projection: Newman projection: a view straight down one C–C bond. The front carbon is a dot with three bonds, the back carbon a circle with three bonds coming from its edge.
glossary.staggered: Staggered: the back carbon's bonds sit halfway between the front carbon's (60° apart). Lower in energy.
glossary.eclipsed: Eclipsed: the back carbon's bonds line up with the front carbon's (0°). Higher in energy (torsional strain).
glossary.gauche: Gauche: two groups 60° apart in a staggered Newman projection. Slightly crowded.
glossary.anti: Anti: two groups 180° apart in a Newman projection. For big groups, the most comfortable position.
glossary.torsional strain: Torsional strain: extra energy from eclipsed bonds pushing against each other.
glossary.trans-diaxial: Trans-diaxial: on neighbouring ring carbons, both bonds axial and pointing opposite ways (one up, one down). The ring version of anti-periplanar, needed for E2 in cyclohexanes.
glossary.axial: Axial: a bond on a chair cyclohexane that points straight up or down, parallel to the ring's axis.
glossary.equatorial: Equatorial: a bond on a chair cyclohexane that points out around the ring's equator. Big groups prefer it.
glossary.E/Z: E/Z: names for C=C geometry using CIP priorities. Z (zusammen): the higher-priority groups on the same side. E (entgegen): opposite sides.
glossary.cis/trans: Cis/trans: same side / opposite sides of a C=C or a ring. Fine for simple cases; E/Z is the general system.
glossary.CIP priority: CIP priority: rank atoms by atomic number (higher wins). On a tie, compare the next atoms out, one layer at a time. Used for R/S and E/Z.
glossary.conjugated: Conjugated: double bonds separated by exactly one single bond (C=C–C=C). The p orbitals overlap along the chain, which adds stability.
glossary.exocyclic: Exocyclic double bond: a C=C with one carbon in a ring and the other outside it.
glossary.dehydration: Dehydration: losing water (H and OH) from an alcohol to make an alkene, usually with H₂SO₄ or H₃PO₄ and heat (E1 at 2°/3°).
glossary.regioselective: Regioselective: one constitutional isomer forms more than the others (e.g. the Zaitsev alkene over the Hofmann one).
glossary.stereoselective: Stereoselective: one stereoisomer forms more than the others when several could (e.g. E over Z in E1).
glossary.heat of hydrogenation: Heat of hydrogenation: the heat released when H₂ adds to a C=C. Less heat = a more stable alkene (compare isomers only).
glossary.β-hydrogen: β-Hydrogen: an H on a carbon next to the carbon with the leaving group (the β-carbon). Elimination removes one.
glossary.α-carbon: α-Carbon (Cα): the carbon that carries the leaving group.
glossary.substrate: Substrate: the molecule that reacts (here, the one with the leaving group).
glossary.aprotic solvent: Polar aprotic solvent: polar but with no O–H or N–H (DMSO, DMF, acetone, CH₃CN). Leaves anions free, so SN2 is fast.
glossary.molecularity: Molecularity: how many species take part in the slow step: 1 = unimolecular (SN1, E1), 2 = bimolecular (SN2, E2).
glossary.rate law: Rate law: how the rate depends on concentrations. SN1/E1: rate = k[substrate]. SN2/E2: rate = k[substrate][Nu or base].
glossary.concerted: Concerted: all bond changes happen in one step, through one transition state (SN2, E2).
